newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: FOCUS - Finland says it now meets all EMU criteria.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Finland says it now meets all EMU criteria.

text.p: Finnish Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto said on Monday his country now meets all the criteria for joining a single currency in 1999 after the weekend move to link the markka to the exchange rate mechanism (ERM).
Niinisto, clearly satisfied with the decision to enter the ERM currency grid, said the Finnish parliament would decide in late 1997 on whether to join economic and monetary union (EMU).
"But I do believe that it will be a positive decision," Niinisto told a press conference, adding he was looking forward to Finland joining the single currency in the first wave.
The EU's monetary committee agreed on Saturday after nearly five hours of talks in Brussels to bring in the markka into the ERM at a central rate of 3.04 against the German mark.
"We are quite satisfied with the rate," Niinisto said.
Explaining the decision, Niinisto said it had become increasingly clear that ERM membership was a condition for joining monetary union.
The other requirements for EMU include limits on government debt and borrowing, inflation and interest rates.

Finland has made huge efforts following the economic crisis of the early 1990s to reduce its budget deficit and bring its debt under control. "The Finnish economy has strengthened a lot," Niinisto said. "We are now fulfilling all the criteria."

The Finnish budget deficit is forecast at 1.4 percent of gross domestic product in 1997, well below the three percent limit set by the EU's Maastricht treaty, while the debt level is forecast to be near the allowed level of 60 percent of GDP.

Niinisto believed the link of the markka to the ERM, which limits currency fluctuations between participating currencies to at most 15 percent up or down, would further increase the economy's stability.
Following the Finnish decision, the grid groups 11 of the 15 EU countries. Only Sweden, Italy, Britain and Greece remain outside.
Italy, desperate to join monetary union, has said it wants to enter the ERM soon and many analysts believe the lira could re-join before the end of the year.
Several countries, including EU heavyweights Germany and France, say membership is needed to qualify for the single currency.
Sweden and Britain, however, insist that it is currency stability, not ERM membership in itself, which should be the key for being able to participate in the single currency.
But some economists say the Finnish decision will increase pressure also on neighbouring Sweden to join the mechanism.
Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink, however, told reporters in Luxembourg on Monday that "there is no increased pressure on Sweden" to join the ERM.

With widespread public opposition to the single currency, Sweden is clearly less enthusiastic about the project than Finland and many analysts believe it will decide to wait with joining EMU even if it were to meet all the criteria.
Asbrink and Niinisto were participating in a meeting of EU finance ministers in Luxembourg.
